What Is FICA Tax? The 7.65% Deduction on Every Paycheck, Explained

Direct AnswerFICA tax is 7.65% of your pay — 6.2% Social Security up to the $184,500 wage base plus 1.45% Medicare. Learn how it works, when it stops, and what it costs.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published October 27, 2026•10 min read•Tax & Payroll Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: 7.65% of Your PayFICA at a Glance: What Applies at Each Wage LevelThe Two Taxes Inside FICAThe FICA FormulasWorked Examples: Three PaychecksFICA vs Federal Income TaxHow to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Quick Answer

FICA tax is 7.65% of your pay — 6.2% Social Security up to the $184,500 wage base, plus 1.45% Medicare.

The Short Answer: 7.65% of Your Pay

FICA is the payroll tax that funds Social Security and Medicare. Every paycheck, your employer withholds 7.65% of your gross pay for it — and then pays a matching 7.65% on top, so the two programs together receive 15.3% of your wages. It is not income tax, it has no brackets, and you cannot adjust it on your W-4. It simply runs on every dollar you earn, with one big exception: the Social Security part stops once your yearly wages pass $184,500.

ComponentYour shareEmployer matchCap
Social Security (OASDI)6.2%6.2%Stops at $184,500 of wages
Medicare (Hospital Insurance)1.45%1.45%No cap — every dollar
Additional Medicare withholding0.9% over $200,000NoneEmployee only
Total FICA7.65%7.65%15.3% combined

If you only remember one thing, make it this: the two lines on your pay stub labeled Social Security and Medicare are not two mysteries — they are FICA, and their rates are fixed. The rest of this guide shows where the money goes, how the cap changes your paycheck late in the year, and how to check your own stub in under a minute.

FICA at a Glance: What Applies at Each Wage Level

FICA does not apply evenly at every income level. The Social Security part switches off at the wage base, while Medicare keeps going — so your effective FICA rate actually falls as your pay rises past the cap:

7.65%

Up to $184,500

Both parts apply: 6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare on every dollar of wages.

1.45%

$184,500 – $200,000

Social Security stops at the wage base; only Medicare keeps running.

2.35%

Over $200,000

Medicare 1.45% plus 0.9% additional Medicare withholding — employee only, no employer match on the extra 0.9%.

In this article: a $60,000 salary pays $4,590 in FICA, while a $250,000 salary pays $15,514 — an effective employee rate of only 6.2%, because the Social Security part stopped at $184,500. The cap is the reason high earners pay a lower FICA percentage than everyone else.

The Two Taxes Inside FICA

FICA looks like one deduction but it is two taxes with different jobs, different rates, and different rules. Splitting them apart is the key to reading your pay stub correctly.

Social Security (OASDI) — 6.2%

OASDI stands for Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance. This is the retirement program most people mean when they say "Social Security": monthly benefits for retired workers, plus benefits for their dependents, survivors of deceased workers, and workers who become disabled. You pay 6.2% and your employer pays 6.2%, for 12.4% combined — but only on wages up to the annual wage base, which is $184,500 for 2026. Every dollar above that is exempt from Social Security tax, which is why your late-year paychecks can suddenly look bigger.

Medicare (Hospital Insurance) — 1.45%

The Medicare part funds Hospital Insurance: inpatient hospital care for people 65 and older and for certain younger people with disabilities. You pay 1.45% and your employer pays 1.45%, for 2.9% combined — on every dollar of wages, with no cap at all. On top of that, an additional 0.9% Medicare tax applies to high earners: your employer must start withholding it once the wages it pays you in the year pass $200,000, and your employer does not match that extra 0.9%.

One distinction worth knowing: the $200,000 withholding trigger is the same for everyone, but the actual tax liability thresholds depend on filing status — $200,000 for single filers, $250,000 for married couples filing jointly, and $125,000 for married filing separately. If your employer withheld the extra 0.9% but your total liability is lower (for example, a joint return under $250,000), the difference is reconciled on your tax return.

Where does the money go? Each part flows into its own federal trust fund, managed by the Treasury. That separation is exactly why the two parts can follow different rules: the Social Security trust funds and the Medicare Hospital Insurance trust fund are accounted for independently, even though both deductions arrive on the same paycheck.

The FICA Formulas

Three formulas cover every employee paycheck. "Wages" here means your Social Security and Medicare wages — usually your gross pay, with the pre-tax exceptions explained in the Limitations section.

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Social SecuritySmaller of (wages, $184,500) × 6.2%Your Social Security withholding
Step 2 — MedicareWages × 1.45%Your Medicare withholding
Step 3 — Additional MedicareWages over $200,000 (per employer) × 0.9%Extra withholding, employee only
TotalStep 1 + Step 2 + Step 3Your FICA for the period

Your employer runs the same three steps with the same rates and sends a matching amount for Steps 1 and 2 — but not Step 3. That is why the combined FICA cost of employing someone is 15.3% of wages below the cap, not 7.65%: the 7.65% you see is only your half.

Worked Examples: Three Paychecks

Each example is verifiable with the three formulas above. All figures assume the full gross amount counts as FICA wages.

Example 1 — $60,000 salary

A $60,000 salary sits entirely below the wage base, so both parts apply to the full amount:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Social Security$60,000 × 6.2%$3,720.00
Step 2 — Medicare$60,000 × 1.45%$870.00
Step 3 — Additional MedicareBelow $200,000$0.00
Total employee FICA$3,720 + $870$4,590.00

Your employer matches $4,590, so the two programs receive $9,180 on a $60,000 salary. This is the same $4,590 FICA line used in our $60,000 after-tax guide — the two articles agree because they use the same 2026 rules.

Example 2 — $2,000 biweekly paycheck

Per paycheck, the same rates apply to the period's gross pay:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Social Security$2,000 × 6.2%$124.00
Step 2 — Medicare$2,000 × 1.45%$29.00
Total per paycheck$124 + $29$153.00

Over 26 biweekly checks, that is $153 × 26 = $3,978 a year — which is exactly the FICA on a $52,000 salary ($2,000 × 26), as in our $25-an-hour after-tax guide. If your stub shows Social Security and Medicare lines, divide each by your gross pay for the period: you should get 6.2% and 1.45%.

Example 3 — $250,000 salary (cap + additional tax)

At $250,000, all three steps matter — and the cap visibly lowers the rate:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Social Security$184,500 × 6.2% (capped)$11,439.00
Step 2 — Medicare$250,000 × 1.45%$3,625.00
Step 3 — Additional Medicare($250,000 − $200,000) × 0.9%$450.00
Total employee FICA$11,439 + $3,625 + $450$15,514.00

Your employer matches Steps 1 and 2 only: $11,439 + $3,625 = $15,064. Combined, the two programs receive $30,578 on a $250,000 salary. Note the effective employee rate: $15,514 ÷ $250,000 = 6.2% — below the headline 7.65% — because $65,500 of this salary escaped Social Security tax entirely. A biweekly-paid $200,000 earner feels the same effect late in the year: the wage base is reached during the 24th check, and the last two checks of the year carry no Social Security withholding at all.

Honesty note: these examples assume every dollar of gross pay counts as FICA wages. Pre-tax health premiums under a cafeteria plan would lower the FICA wages and every figure above; 401(k) contributions would not. See Limitations.

FICA vs Federal Income Tax

The most common confusion on a pay stub is treating FICA as just another income tax. They behave very differently:

FeatureFICAFederal income taxLimitation
Rate shapeFlat: 7.65% (then lower past the cap)Brackets: 10% to 37%FICA has no brackets or standard deduction
CapSocial Security stops at $184,500No capMedicare never stops; income tax never stops
Adjustable on W-4?No — fixed by lawYes — withholding follows your W-4You cannot tune FICA by changing your W-4
What it fundsSocial Security + Medicare onlyGeneral federal spendingSeparate trust funds vs general revenue
Employer matchYes — full 7.65% matchNo matchYour employer's FICA cost is invisible on your stub

That last row matters for job offers: a $60,000 salary costs your employer $64,590 once their $4,590 FICA match is included. When you compare a salaried offer with freelance work, remember the freelancer pays both halves — 15.3% — with no employer covering any of it. Our gross pay vs net pay guide walks through the full journey from gross to take-home.

Limitations

Keep these limits in mind before using any figure above as a budget:

  1. State taxes excluded: state income tax, and in a few states disability insurance, come out separately and are not part of FICA.
  2. Pre-tax deductions are not all equal: health premiums paid through a cafeteria plan reduce Social Security and Medicare wages, but 401(k) contributions do not — they lower income-tax wages only. Your stub's FICA lines may therefore be based on a higher wage figure than your income-tax lines.
  3. Withholding vs liability for the extra 0.9%: employers must withhold it once they pay you over $200,000, but your actual liability depends on filing status ($250,000 joint, $125,000 married filing separately). Any over-withholding is reconciled on your return.
  4. Employees only in this guide: self-employed workers pay both halves as self-employment tax (15.3%) with different deduction rules — the note in the FAQs is a pointer, not a full guide.
  5. Not tax advice: figures use 2026 federal rules. Your return may differ with credits, other income, multiple employers, or tips and other special wage types.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about the FICA lines on their pay stub:

What does FICA stand for?

FICA stands for the Federal Insurance Contributions Act, the law that created the payroll tax funding Social Security and Medicare. When your pay stub shows a Social Security line and a Medicare line, both are FICA taxes — two separate taxes collected together under one law.

How much is FICA tax in 2026?

For most employees, 7.65% of gross pay: 6.2% for Social Security plus 1.45% for Medicare. Your employer matches the full 7.65%, so 15.3% of your wages goes to the two programs combined. Social Security tax stops at the $184,500 wage base; Medicare has no cap, and an extra 0.9% Medicare withholding applies to wages over $200,000.

Is FICA the same as Social Security tax?

No. Social Security tax is only one part of FICA — the 6.2% part. FICA also includes the 1.45% Medicare part. The two programs have separate trust funds and separate rules, which is why the Social Security part can stop at the wage base while the Medicare part keeps running.

Does FICA stop once I earn over $184,500?

Only the Social Security part stops. Once your year-to-date wages pass $184,500, your employer stops withholding the 6.2% Social Security tax and your paycheck gets bigger by that amount for the rest of the year. Medicare withholding at 1.45% continues on every dollar, and above $200,000 an extra 0.9% Medicare withholding starts.

Do self-employed workers pay FICA?

Self-employed workers pay both halves as self-employment tax — 15.3% in total (12.4% Social Security up to the wage base plus 2.9% Medicare) — because there is no employer to pay the matching half. They can deduct half of that tax from their income when figuring adjusted gross income. The full self-employment rules are a separate topic; this article covers employees.

Can I reduce my FICA tax?

Not through your W-4 — FICA rates are fixed by law and do not change with your withholding choices. What can change the amount is the definition of FICA wages: pre-tax health premiums paid through a cafeteria plan reduce Social Security and Medicare wages, while 401(k) contributions do not — they lower income-tax wages only. Beyond that, the only lever is the wage base itself: once your earnings pass $184,500, the Social Security part stops.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • FICA is 7.65% of your pay: 6.2% Social Security + 1.45% Medicare, matched by your employer for 15.3% combined.
  • The $184,500 wage base is the switch: past it, Social Security withholding stops and your paycheck rises — Medicare never stops.
  • Over $200,000, add 0.9%: additional Medicare withholding, employee only, no employer match.
  • 401(k) does not cut FICA: it lowers income-tax wages only; cafeteria-plan health premiums lower FICA wages too.
  • Check your stub in one minute: Social Security ÷ gross pay should be 6.2% (or 0% past the cap); Medicare ÷ gross pay should be 1.45% (or 2.35% past $200,000).
  • For the full picture, read our paycheck tax guide and the after-tax series — $20 an hour, $25 an hour, $50,000, $60,000, and $100,000 — which all link back here for the FICA piece.

Sources & Method

Figures use 2026 federal rules: Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base and Medicare 1.45% with no cap, per IRS Topic No. 751 (Social Security and Medicare withholding rates); additional Medicare withholding above $200,000 of employer-paid wages, with liability thresholds of $250,000 (married filing jointly) and $125,000 (married filing separately). Worked examples were recomputed from the formulas in this article and cross-checked against the FICA lines in the site's after-tax series ($60,000 → $4,590; $52,000 → $3,978; $100,000 → $7,650). State income tax, retirement contributions, health premiums, bonuses, and overtime are excluded except where a pre-tax note says otherwise. This article is general information, not tax advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. Social Security is 6.2% up to the $184,500 wage base — earnings above that base are no longer charged the Social Security part.
  2. Medicare is 1.45% of your pay.
  3. FICA is separate from federal income tax — it funds Social Security and Medicare.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated October 27, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
